item.title: Server
item.description:
claimward-vpn-server v0.10.0 is the control plane. It verifies the bearer a device presents, allocates VPN addresses, and programs the WireGuard gateway with one peer per enrolled device. It runs on the gateway host, beside an existing wg0: Linux (nftables) or, from v0.10.0, OpenBSD (pf, see OpenBSD).

What it serves

Listener Path Purpose
LISTEN_ADDR (:8443) POST /api/v1/enroll verify, choose the tenant, allocate an address, add the peer, return the tunnel configuration
GET /api/v1/tenants the tenants the caller may connect to
POST /api/v1/heartbeat renew the device’s lease
POST /api/v1/deregister remove the peer
GET /healthz liveness
/admin/ admin API and WebUI, when the admin-token credential exists
GRPC_ADDR (:8444) claimward.routes.v1.RouteService/Watch streams the tenant’s routes and their updates
METRICS_ADDR (no default: off unless set) GET /metrics Prometheus metrics, on a listener of their own, never on LISTEN_ADDR

The API requests carry Authorization: Bearer <token>: a GitHub access token, an OIDC ID token, or a go-authn access token, depending on AUTH_PROVIDER. See the enrollment protocol for the payloads.

With TLS_CERT and TLS_KEY both listeners use TLS. Without them the HTTP API is plain (terminate TLS at a proxy), and so is the RouteService, which the clients then refuse except on loopback: devices connect, but get no live route updates.

Configuration

Settings are in the environment. Secrets are not: since v0.6.0 they are files in a credentials directory, see Credentials below.

Variable Required Default Notes
AUTH_PROVIDER github identity provider: github, oidc or go-authn
GITHUB_ALLOWED_ORGS github — CSV organisation allowlist: an active member of any is allowed, and so is a named tenant member. Since v0.5.0 it is optional only when at least one tenant has members: with neither the server refuses to start, with no opt-out (before: required since v0.4.0)
GITHUB_API_URL https://api.github.com set for GitHub Enterprise
OIDC_ISSUER oidc, go-authn — issuer URL (discovery)
OIDC_CLIENT_ID oidc, go-authn — the audience tokens must carry
OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS — CSV email-domain allowlist (oidc); the token’s email must be verified
GOAUTHN_GATEWAY_CLIENT_ID go-authn — the gateway’s own client at the provider (wireguard_peers)
GOAUTHN_PEER_LIST_INTERVAL 30s how often the list of registered keys is fetched
GOAUTHN_SSF false also poll the provider’s Shared Signals stream, so that a disabling is acted on at once; the gateway’s client must be an SSF receiver there
GOAUTHN_SSF_INTERVAL 5s how often the SSF stream is polled
WG_ENDPOINT ✅ — public host:port of the gateway, advertised to clients
CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY ✅ — the directory that holds the secret files, see Credentials
WG_INTERFACE wg0 interface to manage
WG_DRYRUN false log peer operations instead of applying them (local development)
VPN_CIDR 10.80.0.0/24 IPv4 address pool; its first host is the gateway’s
PUSH_ROUTES VPN_CIDR CSV routes of the default tenant
DNS — CSV DNS servers of the default tenant
TENANTS_FILE — JSON file of tenants loaded at start, with their access policy
KEEPALIVE 25 persistent keepalive advertised to clients (seconds)
LEASE_TTL 24h how long an enrollment lasts without a heartbeat
TUNNEL_MTU derived MTU of the WireGuard interface, 1280 to 9000, advertised as mtu; anything else refuses to start. Unset: the uplink MTU minus 80, at most 1420, at least 1280. The same atomic inet claimward table also clamps the MSS of every TCP SYN crossing the interface (forwarded both ways, and input for the gateway itself) to this MTU minus 40 (IPv4) or 60 (IPv6)
LISTEN_ADDR :8443 HTTP listen address
GRPC_ADDR :8444 RouteService listen address; Watch streams are re-authorised every 15 s and end when the identity is no longer allowed
METRICS_ADDR — (off) separate listener for /metrics, served only when set (since v0.9.0 there is no default port: the old 127.0.0.1:9090 clashed with Prometheus); never on LISTEN_ADDR. It names every tenant: keep it on loopback or a private network
MAX_DEVICES_PER_SUBJECT 5 devices one identity may enroll
GRPC_ENDPOINT — host:port of the RouteService advertised to clients; empty, they do not watch
TLS_CERT / TLS_KEY — HTTPS, and TLS on the RouteService
DEBUG — any value: debug logging (one line per request)

Credentials

Every secret is a file in the directory named by CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY, never an environment variable: an environment is copied into every child process and every crash dump. systemd sets the variable for LoadCredential= and LoadCredentialEncrypted=; on the other platforms you set it yourself. The file names are fixed, and one trailing newline is trimmed.

File Required Content
wg-private-key always the gateway’s base64 private key
admin-token no bearer of the admin API and WebUI; without the file they are disabled
goauthn-gateway-secret AUTH_PROVIDER=go-authn the gateway client’s secret
github-token when any tenant has members bearer for GET /users/{login} (see Tenants)

A missing required file stops the start and names the file. Before reading, the server checks each file through its open descriptor (O_NOFOLLOW, then fstat) and refuses a symbolic link, anything but a regular file, a file readable by group or other, a file not owned by the server’s uid, an empty file and one over 64 KiB. One exception since v0.7.1: a file owned by uid 0 with mode exactly 0440 is accepted when its group is the server’s gid or one of its supplementary groups (what a Kubernetes Secret volume with fsGroup produces). A second one since v0.9.0, for systemd with DynamicUser=yes: systemd leaves the file root:root, mode 0400, plus a read-only POSIX ACL entry for the service’s uid (src/core/exec-credential.c:338-361, src/shared/acl-util.c:448-494), so stat shows 0440. The server reads system.posix_acl_access from the open descriptor and accepts exactly user:: (no write or execute), user:<its uid>:r--, group::---, mask::r--, other::---; any other named user or group, any write or execute bit, or a malformed or oversized value is refused. The error gives the fix.

Platform CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY Owner and mode
systemd set by LoadCredentialEncrypted= with DynamicUser=yes (as shipped): root-owned with a read-only ACL for the service’s uid, accepted; with a fixed User= on a filesystem without ACLs: the service user, 0400. Private tmpfs
Docker Swarm /run/secrets, set by hand mode: 0400 on the secret
Docker Compose /run/secrets, set by hand the host file’s: chown and chmod 0400 it, and set user: to match
Podman /run/secrets, set by hand --secret ...,mode=0400 (Quadlet: Secret=...,mode=0400)
Kubernetes the Secret volume’s mount path, set by hand defaultMode: 0440 and fsGroup: the files are root:<fsGroup>, accepted by the group rule above, so the pod runs as a non-root uid with every capability dropped but NET_ADMIN. add: [NET_ADMIN] alone does not give a non-root uid the capability (no ambient set): the image’s binary needs setcap cap_net_admin=+ep (per capabilities(7), not measured on a cluster)
s6 (no systemd) /run/sdcreds/claimward-server, set by sdcreds s6-run the service user, 0400, in a private tmpfs (see s6)
otherwise any directory chmod 0400, owned by the service user

Ready-made units for systemd, Compose, Podman, Kubernetes and s6 are in the repository’s deploy/ directory, with the systemd-creds encrypt steps. Hosts without systemd get the same directory from go-authn/sdcreds (see s6); the server does not depend on it.

The organisation check of the github provider does not use github-token: it runs with the person’s token, so a private membership is visible only if that token carries read:org. The credential is optional while only organisations are used.

Migrating from v0.5.0 (breaking). ADMIN_TOKEN, WG_PRIVATE_KEY, WG_PRIVATE_KEY_FILE and GOAUTHN_GATEWAY_SECRET_FILE are no longer read, and the server refuses to start while one of them is set, naming the file to create. Put each value in its file (admin-token, wg-private-key, goauthn-gateway-secret), unset the variable and set CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY. A tenant with members now also needs github-token.

Authentication providers

Authentication is pluggable behind the Verifier interface (internal/auth):

  • github (default): the bearer is a GitHub OAuth access token from the device flow. The server resolves it through the GitHub API (/user, /user/orgs) and, with GITHUB_ALLOWED_ORGS, admits an active member of one of those organisations, or a named tenant member (the list is optional only when a tenant has members). No client secret is involved.
  • oidc: the bearer is an OIDC ID token, verified against the issuer with the audience OIDC_CLIENT_ID and the optional email-domain allowlist.
  • go-authn: the bearer is an access token (at+jwt) from a go-authn/bridge provider, and the device’s key must be registered there by the same person. The server reads the provider’s signed list of registered keys (go-authn/wireguard) and drops from wg0 a key the provider takes back.

See Identity providers for each flow end to end.

Enrollment rules

  • A key belongs to whoever enrolled it. Enrolling a key another identity holds is refused (409 key_taken): a public key is public, and taking one over would give the power to deregister its owner’s device.
  • The same key enrolled again by its owner keeps its address and gets a new lease.
  • The peer’s only allowed IP is the device’s /32, so devices cannot use each other’s addresses.
  • The tenant is the one the caller asked for, if they are a member, or their only one. See Tenants.

How it programs the gateway

The server uses wgctrl to add and remove peers on an existing interface, and checks at start-up that the interface exists. The interface itself (its private key and listen port) is left to wg-quick or systemd-networkd at boot, which keeps the privileged interface setup out of the long-running service.

OpenBSD (pf)

From v0.10.0 the server also runs on OpenBSD, where it enforces the access policy with pf instead of nftables. It talks to the kernel directly through the /dev/pf ioctls; it never runs pfctl, and there is no pfctl fallback.

  • Supported releases: OpenBSD 7.9 and 8.0. They share one struct pf_rule layout, which the server checks against the running release. On any other release the server refuses to start rather than risk encoding a rule wrongly.

  • You own pf.conf. The server never edits the main ruleset. Add one line to /etc/pf.conf and keep pf enabled:

    anchor "claimward"

    The server loads the policy into that anchor. At start it reads the main ruleset back and verifies that it calls anchor "claimward".

  • It refuses to start when /dev/pf cannot be opened read-write (it must start as root), when pf is disabled, when the main ruleset does not call the anchor (the policy would be loaded and filter nothing), and when pf.conf has set skip on for the WireGuard interface (wg0, wg*), because pf would then never see the peers’ traffic.

  • Same policy as on Linux. Default deny on traffic arriving on WG_INTERFACE; only IPv4 is allowed, and IPv6 across the tunnel is dropped. The MSS clamp (TUNNEL_MTU) covers both families, as a match ... scrub (max-mss N) rule.

  • Atomic and fail closed. The anchor and its tables are replaced in one pf transaction, then read back and compared with what was meant to be loaded. If that fails, deny-all is loaded. The anchor stays in place when the process exits. Table names carry a per-load generation suffix, so that the short window between the table commit and the rule commit can never apply one tenant’s rules to another tenant’s peers.

  • Privilege separation (from v0.11.0). The pf promise of pledge(2) lets a process issue only twelve of the DIOC* ioctls (sys/kern/kern_pledge.c, pledge_ioctl), and the server also needs DIOCRINADEFINE, DIOCXROLLBACK, DIOCGETRULES, DIOCGETRULE, DIOCXEND and DIOCRGETADDRS; any other ioctl would kill the process. So the root parent, which drives /dev/pf, is not pledged. The unprivileged _claimward child, which holds the secrets and serves the network, is restricted with unveil(2) and pledge(2) before it serves (see below).

  • WireGuard peers (from v0.11.0). Before v0.11.0 an enrolment on OpenBSD failed when it added the peer to wg(4) (issue #79). The server now writes peers with the SIOCSWG and SIOCGWG ioctls of sys/net/if_wg.h and reads them back with its own decoder. Verified in real OpenBSD 7.9 and 8.0 amd64 virtual machines: the structure layout matches the C compiler’s, and add, replace, remove and sweep work on a real wg(4) interface. OpenBSD on arm64 is only cross-compiled, not run on a kernel.

Deploying on OpenBSD (rc.d)

From v0.10.1 the repository ships deploy/openbsd/: an rc.d(8) script, an environment.example, a hostname.wg0.example and a pf.conf.example.

  • Two processes (from v0.11.0). The WireGuard peer configuration of wg(4) is behind suser(9) (sys/net/if_wg.c), and /dev/pf is guarded only by its device node, which is root-only: pfopen (sys/net/pf_ioctl.c) checks nothing else. OpenBSD has no privileged group that would let an unprivileged user do either, so the script starts the daemon as root (daemon_user="root") and the daemon splits in two. The parent (root) adds and removes peers, sets the tunnel MTU and loads the pf anchor; it reads no credential, serves no network and unveil(2)s only /dev/pf. The child, run as the _claimward user, holds the secrets, the TLS and gRPC listeners, the identity provider and the tenant policy, and is restricted with unveil(2) and pledge(2) (stdio rpath inet dns) before it serves. If it cannot drop privileges, the server does not start. The child asks the parent through a socketpair, and the parent refuses anything outside the address pool (VPN_CIDR).
  • The _claimward user must exist and the ports must be above 1024 (the defaults 8443 and 8444 are); to serve on 443, redirect it with a pf rdr-to.
  • Secrets are files in /etc/claimward/credentials, a 0700 directory owned by _claimward, with each file 0400 and owned by _claimward (install(1)). The script sets CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY to it; no secret goes in the environment, in arguments or in a URL. The non-secret settings are in /etc/claimward/environment, which stays root’s.
  • wg0 must exist before the server starts: hostname.wg0 carries the same private key as the wg-private-key credential (mode 0640).
install -m 0555 claimward-server /usr/local/bin/claimward-server
useradd -g =uid -c claimward -d /var/empty -s /sbin/nologin -r 1..999 _claimward
install -d -m 0755 -o root -g wheel /etc/claimward
install -d -m 0700 -o _claimward -g _claimward /etc/claimward/credentials
install -m 0400 -o _claimward -g _claimward wg-private-key /etc/claimward/credentials/wg-private-key
install -m 0600 -o root -g wheel environment.example /etc/claimward/environment # then edit
install -m 0640 -o root -g wheel hostname.wg0.example /etc/hostname.wg0 # then edit
sh /etc/netstart wg0
install -m 0555 claimward_server /etc/rc.d/claimward_server
rcctl enable claimward_server
rcctl start claimward_server && rcctl check claimward_server

rcctl start reports (ok) only once the server accepts connections on LISTEN_ADDR; a daemon that exits first, for instance on a credential the _claimward account does not own, is (failed).

The log goes to syslog (/var/log/daemon). The CI runs this script in real OpenBSD 7.9 and 8.0 virtual machines: rcctl start, the startup line, rcctl check, a root parent with one _claimward child, an enrolment through the child whose peer appears on wg0, and rcctl stop; then a start with a credential owned by root, and a start without the anchor in pf.conf, which must both fail.

Deploying under s6 (sdcreds)

From v0.10.2 the repository ships deploy/s6/claimward-server/ (run and finish) for hosts without systemd. sdcreds s6-run (go-authn/sdcreds v0.2.0 or later) decrypts every file of its --source directory into a private tmpfs, writes each one 0400 and owned by --user, sets CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY, and starts the server as that user. A file owned by the process’s own uid with no group or other access is the first shape the loader accepts, so the loader is unchanged. Nothing secret goes in the environment, in argv or in a URL.

  • One capability, kept on purpose. The server needs CAP_NET_ADMIN (wgctrl, nftables, the interface MTU). s6-run empties every capability set of the service by default and keeps no_new_privs; the example passes --keep-cap=CAP_NET_ADMIN, so the server runs with exactly that one (CapEff 0x1000). The capability acts on the network namespace the supervision tree runs in: the host’s, unless you start s6-svscan inside one of its own (ip netns exec).
  • Names. Each file of --source is named like its credential (wg-private-key, github-token, admin-token, goauthn-gateway-secret) and encrypted with sdcreds encrypt --name=<that name>; any other name stops the start. s6-run needs root and CAP_SYS_ADMIN (it mounts).
  • Configuration that is not secret goes in /etc/claimward/env, read by the run script.
  • Containers do not need it: Compose, Podman and Kubernetes mount secrets as files already (table above).

The CI runs this directory under a real s6-svscan, in a network namespace with a real WireGuard link and nftables (not a dry run). It checks that the log holds the public key derived from the encrypted credential (and not a control key), that the server runs as the service user with CapEff 0x1000 and no_new_privs, that no secret is in its environment, that a credential file with mode 0644 is refused, and that stopping the service removes the mount.

Run locally

With WG_DRYRUN=true no WireGuard device is touched:

export AUTH_PROVIDER=oidc
export OIDC_ISSUER=https://accounts.google.com
export OIDC_CLIENT_ID=xxxx.apps.googleusercontent.com
export WG_ENDPOINT=vpn.example.com:51820
export CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY=$HOME/.local/state/claimward-dev-creds
(umask 077; mkdir -p "$CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY"; wg genkey > "$CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY/wg-private-key")
chmod 0400 "$CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY/wg-private-key"
export WG_DRYRUN=true LISTEN_ADDR=:8080

go run ./cmd/claimward-server

task run:dev does the same with GitHub sign-in and an ephemeral key, and task dex runs a local Dex to sign in against (deploy/dev/).

Run behind TLS. Bearer tokens are credentials: always serve the API over HTTPS, either with TLS_CERT/TLS_KEY or behind a TLS-terminating proxy, and give the RouteService a certificate so that devices get live route updates.

item.title: Identity providers
item.description:
The server and the apps each select a provider by name, and must agree: AUTH_PROVIDER on the server, "provider" in the app’s config.json (or CLAIMWARD_AUTH_PROVIDER). The bearer the app obtains is opaque on the wire; how the server verifies it depends on the provider.

Provider Sign-in on the device Bearer sent to the server How the server verifies it
github (default) OAuth device flow GitHub OAuth access token GitHub API (/user, /user/orgs), optional organisation allowlist
oidc authorization code + PKCE, in the browser OIDC ID token signature, issuer, audience; optional email-domain allowlist
go-authn device flow, then key registration go-authn access token (at+jwt) signature, issuer, audience, typ; the key must be registered by the same subject

GitHub

The default. The app runs the GitHub device flow: it shows a code and the page where to enter it, and opens that page in the browser. Only a client ID is needed, no secret, so create a GitHub OAuth App with Device Flow enabled. The app asks for read:user, user:email and read:org.

The server resolves the person through the GitHub API with their token: their numeric ID is the subject (github:<id>), their organisations (/user/orgs) are their groups for tenants, and their public email, when they have one, counts as verified. With GITHUB_ALLOWED_ORGS, an active membership of one of those organisations admits them, and so does being a named members entry of a tenant (pinned to the account ID, see tenants). The allowlist is optional only when a tenant has members: with neither, the server refuses to start. Set GITHUB_API_URL for GitHub Enterprise.

AUTH_PROVIDER=github
GITHUB_ALLOWED_ORGS=my-org,my-other-org

OpenID Connect

AUTH_PROVIDER=oidc with OIDC_ISSUER (discovered through /.well-known/openid-configuration) and OIDC_CLIENT_ID, the audience the ID token must carry. The app runs the authorization code flow with PKCE: it opens the browser and receives the redirect on http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback, with a port chosen at each sign-in. It asks for openid profile email offline_access. Register a public/native client, without a secret.

The server takes the subject, the email and email_verified, the preferred_username and the groups claim (a list, or a single string). With OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS, the email’s domain must be one of those.

go-authn

go-authn/bridge is an OpenID Connect provider in front of a SAML federation (RENATER, eduGAIN). It also keeps whose each WireGuard key is, so a valid token is no longer enough to enroll a device:

  1. The app signs in with the provider’s device flow, scope openid wireguard. That token opens the provider’s key registry and nothing else: the provider addresses a token carrying one of its own scopes to itself alone.
  2. At every connection the app registers the device’s public key (POST /wireguard/key), which renews it when it is already the person’s, then refreshes for scope=openid alone. That gives an access token addressed to the VPN server. The provider rotates refresh tokens, and the app keeps the new one. The private key never leaves the device.
  3. The server accepts only an access token (typ: at+jwt, RFC 9068) whose audience is OIDC_CLIENT_ID, never an ID token. It enrolls the key only if the provider’s list has it registered by the same subject; otherwise it answers 403 key_not_registered. A lease never outlives the key’s registration.

The list comes from go-authn/wireguard:

  • it is fetched with the gateway’s own client (client_credentials, scope wireguard_peers) and signed by the provider for that gateway alone (typ: wireguard-peers+jwt);
  • it is fetched again every GOAUTHN_PEER_LIST_INTERVAL (30 seconds by default). A key the provider takes back (the person or their institution disabled, or the device removed) is dropped from wg0 at the next fetch, and its heartbeat is refused;
  • a list older than one already seen is refused, which is the replay protection;
  • it fails closed: a list is valid five minutes, and past that the gateway admits nobody new, while tunnels already up end with their leases;
  • the first list is fetched before the server listens: a gateway that cannot read it does not start;
  • with GOAUTHN_SSF=true, the gateway also polls the provider’s Shared Signals stream (SSF 1.0, poll delivery, RFC 8936) every GOAUTHN_SSF_INTERVAL. An event only makes the list be fetched at once: it is a trigger, never a decision, so a forged event buys one extra fetch and nothing else.

Tenants are matched on the token’s groups (eduPerson entitlements) and idp (the entity ID of the institution that vouched), and on the email’s domain only when the provider verified the address.

Configuration

On the server:

AUTH_PROVIDER=go-authn
OIDC_ISSUER=https://login.example.org
OIDC_CLIENT_ID=claimward # the audience of the access tokens
GOAUTHN_GATEWAY_CLIENT_ID=claimward-gw # the gateway's own client
CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY=/etc/claimward/credentials # holds wg-private-key and goauthn-gateway-secret (the gateway's secret, a file only)
GOAUTHN_SSF=true # optional

At the provider (go-authn/bridge’s configuration):

wireguard {
 lifetime = "24h" # a key is listed this long; registering it again renews it
 max_keys = 10 # devices per person
}

client "claimward" { # the client people sign in with
 device = true
 wireguard_keys = true # its tokens, with the wireguard scope, may register a key
 refresh_lifetime = "720h"
}

client "claimward-gw" { # the gateway's own client
 secret_file = "/etc/bridge/claimward-gw.secret"
 wireguard_peers = ["claimward"] # it reads the keys registered through these clients
 ssf_receiver = true # optional: told at once when somebody is disabled
}

In the app’s config.json:

{
 "server_url": "https://vpn.example.com",
 "provider": "go-authn",
 "oidc_issuer": "https://login.example.org",
 "oidc_client_id": "claimward"
}

Adding a provider

On the server, implement Verifier (internal/auth) and register it in auth.New. On the client, implement Provider (pkg/auth) and register it in auth.New; a provider that keeps the devices’ keys itself also implements KeyRegistrar.
